cards.explanation: Their complaint is that their widows are being overlooked. The Grecian Jews say their widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food. It's a grumble about real people getting missed. I think that's why the Twelve, Jesus' apostles, don't wave it off and call a meeting instead.

The answer is the word of God. The Twelve say, “It is unacceptable for us to neglect the word of God in order to wait on tables.” They aren't calling the table work small, friends. They're saying the word of God can't be the thing that gets dropped. I've dropped a whole tray of dough once, so I know how it feels when something important hits the floor.

The answer is seven! The Twelve say, “…select from among you seven men confirmed to be full of the Spirit and wisdom.” Later in verse 5 the group chooses seven names, so the number holds all the way through.

The answer is prayer. The Twelve say they “…will devote ourselves to prayer and to the ministry of the word.” Those two go together in their plan, friends. Once the seven take the food, the apostles can give those two their full attention.

The answer is Stephen, one of the seven, and he gets named first. He's described as “…a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit…” Remember that name, friends, because he's the one this whole passage ends up following. He'll be in the spotlight soon.
The answer is False. The text says the apostles “…prayed and laid their hands on them.” No oil is mentioned in this passage. It's two plain things, friends: prayer and hands laid on the seven.

The answer is True! Verse 7 says, “The number of disciples in Jerusalem grew rapidly, and a great number of priests became obedient to the faith.” Priests are in the number, not only the crowd. The word of God kept spreading, and it wasn't slowing down.

The answer is that they can't stand up to his wisdom. The text says, “…they could not stand up to his wisdom or the Spirit by whom he spoke.” It's a whole group against Stephen, and they can't hold their ground. I've argued with a timer and lost, so I know the feeling.

The answer is True. The text says they prompted some men to say, and those men say, “We heard Stephen speak words of blasphemy against Moses and against God.” So the men from the synagogue get others to say it. Blasphemy means speaking against God, which is a heavy thing to say about a man.

The answer is the Sanhedrin, Israel's ruling council. Verse 12 says, “They seized him and brought him before the Sanhedrin…” They stir up the people, elders and scribes first, and then they grab him. This is a hard moment for Stephen, and I think it would be for anyone.

The answer is this holy place and the law. The false witnesses say, “This man never stops speaking against this holy place and against the law.” The text calls them false witnesses, friends, so this charge isn't true. It's a heavy moment, so I'll just say it plainly.

The answer is False. The witnesses say, “…we have heard him say that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place…” In their claim, Stephen isn't the one doing it. They add that Jesus will “…change the customs that Moses handed down to us.”

The answer is a face like an angel's. Verse 15 says, “…they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.” This is while Stephen is standing accused by false witnesses. I think that's the kind of thing you'd stare at, friends, and the text says they looked intently.
